annotations.text:
Two CRT eras, not a colour inversion.

Dark is a warm amber phosphor tube. Light is the cool monochrome
screen that came after it — a blue-white display with near-black
blue letters, the way an early all-in-one looked.

The axis between them is temperature, not brightness. That is what
makes them siblings instead of one being the other with the lights
turned on.

Deliberately NOT paper: no cream, no warm off-white, no ivory. The
ground stays a screen the whole way through, because the product is
a screen.

All four show the same moment: one line typed, a miss on the next,
the rest still to come.

The number that matters is the untyped text, because that is what
you have to read in order to type it.

  Amber phosphor          1.96:1   below AA — kept as-is
  Amber high contrast     7.73:1   clears AAA
  Monochrome screen       4.73:1   clears AA
  Screen high contrast    9.09:1   clears AAA

Both high-contrast themes clear AAA on every token, syntax colours
included. Every value was computed against its own background.

How the picker handles its own contrast:

The whole page adopts a theme as you move between them, so you are
choosing by seeing rather than by reading a label. A swatch cannot
tell you what typing in a theme feels like; the page can.

The picker chrome and the start button stay on the high-contrast
token set of whichever scheme is showing. So even while the amber
phosphor theme is previewing at 1.96:1, the control you need in
order to leave it stays legible.

The opening guess comes from the system — prefers-color-scheme picks
the pair, prefers-contrast: more picks the high-contrast one of that
pair — so for most people the highlighted card is already right and
the picker only has to confirm.
